title: Jeremiah 30:1–11
context: Chapters 30–33 are often called the book of consolation. The narrator introduces the LORD’s word to Jeremiah (30:1), and the LORD tells him to write all his words in a book (30:2; compare 36:2), because the days are coming when he will reverse the captivity of Israel and Judah and bring them back to the land given to their fathers (30:3). In 30:5–7 the LORD voices a cry of trembling: men clutch their waists like women in labor, faces turn pale, and the day is called “the time of Jacob’s trouble; but he will be saved out of it.” Readers take this in several ways: many see the Babylonian crisis and the return from exile; some see that history as a pattern fulfilled more fully in Christ and the trials of his people; others, especially futurist readers, expect a future time of distress for Israel before final deliverance. These views run across both traditions rather than dividing them, and the notes present them without choosing. In 30:8–9 the LORD promises to break the yoke (compare the yoke of chapters 27–28) and to raise up “David their king,” which many readers in both traditions hear messianically (compare 23:5–6; Ezekiel 34:23–24; 37:24–25; Hosea 3:5); the Davidic covenant is treated as shared ground, as at 2 Samuel 7. Jeremiah 30:10–11 reappears, with small differences in wording, in 46:27–28; the two are named here without merging the two settings.

verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator introduces a new section: “The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD.” Arminian readers note that the consolation that follows comes by the same prophetic word that announced judgment, so hope is not a human invention but a gracious initiative God offers to a people who must still receive it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also stress that the word comes “from the LORD,” so the restoration promised in chapters 30–33 rests on his purpose rather than on Judah’s condition. Shared ground: both traditions read the heading as marking divine revelation, and both see judgment and hope coming from the same faithful God.

verses.text: “The LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘Write all the words that I have spoken to you in a book.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah to “Write all the words that I have spoken to you in a book.” Arminian readers see the writing as a gift to later generations, especially the exiles, who could read the promises and respond in faith long after the prophet spoke (compare 36:2, where a scroll is also commanded).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the command as God securing his word for the people he intends to restore, so the promise outlasts the collapse of the nation. Shared ground: both traditions value the written word as the lasting form of revelation, and both read the book as meant to sustain hope through the exile.

verses.text: For, behold, the days come,’ says the LORD, ‘that I will reverse the captivity of my people Israel and Judah,’ says the LORD. ‘I will cause them to return to the land that I gave to their fathers, and they will possess it.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises to “reverse the captivity of my people Israel and Judah” and bring them back to the land given to their fathers. Arminian readers see covenant faithfulness that keeps its promises to the fathers, and they note that both kingdoms are named, so northern Israel is not forgotten. The promise invites the scattered to trust and return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same promise as the LORD’s sovereign pledge: “I will cause them to return.” The restoration depends on his initiative, not on the exiles’ strength. Shared ground: both traditions hear the land promise to the fathers (compare Genesis 15:18) behind the verse, and both see Israel and Judah reunited in God’s purpose (compare 3:18).

verses.text: These are the words that the LORD spoke concerning Israel and concerning Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator marks these as words the LORD spoke “concerning Israel and concerning Judah.” Arminian readers note again that the whole covenant people is in view, the northern tribes long scattered as well as Judah, which shows the breadth of God’s concern and his willingness to restore those who had seemed lost.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the whole people of God in view and read the double naming as a sign that the LORD’s purpose to gather his people spans both houses. Shared ground: both traditions take the reunion of Israel and Judah as a recurring hope in Jeremiah (compare 3:18; 31:27, 31) and in other prophets (compare Ezekiel 37:15–22).

verses.text: For the LORD says: “We have heard a voice of trembling; a voice of fear, and not of peace.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD voices the cry of the people: “We have heard a voice of trembling; a voice of fear, and not of peace.” Arminian readers hear the terror of a people facing the judgment they were warned about, and they note that the false prophets’ promise of peace has collapsed (compare 6:14), leaving room for honest repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same terror and see God exposing the emptiness of false security before he brings salvation, so that deliverance will be known as his work. Shared ground: both traditions read the trembling as the real fear of judgment, and both see the contrast with “peace” as answering the false prophets Jeremiah opposed (compare 8:11; 23:17).

verses.text: Ask now, and see whether a man travails with child. Why do I see every man with his hands on his waist, as a woman in travail, and all faces are turned pale?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks whether a man can travail with child, then pictures every man with hands on his waist like a woman in labor, all faces pale. Arminian readers see a vivid image of helpless anguish: strong men undone by the coming disaster. They note that labor imagery also hints at something to be born beyond the pain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same image of utter helplessness, which strips away human strength so that the deliverance promised in 30:7 rests on God alone. Shared ground: both traditions read the labor image as anguish rather than literal physiology, and both note that Jeremiah uses similar imagery elsewhere (compare 4:31; 6:24; 22:23).

verses.text: Alas, for that day is great, so that none is like it! It is even the time of Jacob’s trouble; but he will be saved out of it.
verses.arminianNotes: “It is even the time of Jacob’s trouble; but he will be saved out of it.” Arminian readers hold together real distress and a sure promise of rescue. Many see the Babylonian crisis and the return; some see a pattern fulfilled in Christ; some expect a future time of distress for Israel. Readers in this tradition hold each of these views, and the text does not require only one.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hold the trouble as real and the rescue as certain, grounded in God’s promise that “he will be saved out of it.” Many see the exile and return, many read the pattern typologically in Christ and his church, and some expect a future fulfillment for Israel. Shared ground: both traditions stress salvation “out of” trouble, not escape from it, and neither divides over the timing.

verses.text: It will come to pass in that day, says the LORD of Armies, that I will break his yoke from off your neck, and will burst your bonds. Strangers will no more make them their bondservants;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies promises to break the yoke from off their neck and burst their bonds, so strangers will no more make them bondservants. Arminian readers hear an echo of the yoke of chapters 27–28 and see God freeing his people from foreign domination, a liberation that calls for grateful service in return (30:9).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the yoke broken by God’s own hand, so freedom is his gift rather than Judah’s achievement, and many hear it as a picture of deeper deliverance from bondage. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a reversal of the yoke Jeremiah once wore and announced (compare 27:2; 28:10–14), and both see the promise as grace.

verses.text: but they will serve the LORD their God, and David their king, whom I will raise up to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Freed from strangers, “they will serve the LORD their God, and David their king, whom I will raise up to them.” Arminian readers, like many in both traditions, hear the promise of a coming son of David and see it fulfilled in Christ, while recognizing that it first addressed a people without a king. Service to God and his king is the free response of the redeemed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise root the promise in the Davidic covenant of 2 Samuel 7 and commonly read it as fulfilled in Christ, the Son of David (compare 23:5–6; Ezekiel 34:23–24; 37:24–25; Hosea 3:5). Shared ground: the messianic reading is widely held in both traditions, and both see liberation from the yoke leading into service, not into autonomy.

verses.text: Therefore don’t be afraid, O Jacob my servant, says the LORD. Don’t be dismayed, Israel. For, behold, I will save you from afar, and save your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob will return, and will be quiet and at ease. No one will make him afraid.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore don’t be afraid, O Jacob my servant, says the LORD.” The LORD promises to save Israel from afar and bring their offspring from captivity, so that Jacob will return and be at ease. Arminian readers see tender reassurance meant to awaken trust in the exiles, inviting them to rest in God’s promise even before they see it (compare Isaiah 41:8–10).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same reassurance grounded in God’s choice of Jacob as “my servant,” so the promise stands because of his commitment, not theirs. Shared ground: both traditions hear the comfort as real and personal, and both note that 30:10–11 reappears, with small differences in wording, in 46:27–28, which is named here without merging the two settings.

verses.text: For I am with you, says the LORD, to save you; for I will make a full end of all the nations where I have scattered you, but I will not make a full end of you; but I will correct you in measure, and will in no way leave you unpunished.”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will make a full end of all the nations where I have scattered you, but I will not make a full end of you; but I will correct you in measure.” Arminian readers see judgment and mercy held together: discipline is real and deserved, yet measured and aimed at restoration, which invites the people to receive correction rather than resist it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God preserving his people through judgment, correcting them as a father rather than destroying them as enemies (compare Hebrews 12:6). Shared ground: both traditions hear the refrain “not … a full end” (compare 4:27; 5:10, 18) as covenant mercy, and both hold that the LORD will “in no way leave you unpunished,” so mercy never cancels justice.
